REQUESTS FOR TRANSFER TO CANADA OF SOLDIERS BURIED OVERSEAS
speechtext:
1.	Have requests been made to the government by certain Canadian families with a view to repatriating the bodies of the members of such families who died during world war II and were buried overseas?
2.	Were arrangements made for meeting such requests?
3.	If not, for what reasons?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: REQUESTS FOR TRANSFER TO CANADA OF SOLDIERS BURIED OVERSEAS
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	No.
3.	The question of repatriation of war dead to their respective countries received most sympathetic consideration by the governments of the countries of the commonwealth during and at the conclusion of the great war, 1914-18. At that time, it was decided by all the commonwealth countries that all should remain together in the cemeteries
(Mr. MacNaught.]
which would be attended by the war graves commission acting in the interest of all. After the most serious consideration by all the governments concerned, the same policy has been continued in respect to the fallen of the second world war. While representations have been received from individual next of kin seeking to bring the remains of the fallen to this side, these have been relatively few in number and there can be no doubt but that the policy adopted has met with the support of the vast majority of relatives. Undoubtedly, one reason for this has been that it has been applied without a single known exception ever since 1914.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
subsubtopic: WOMEN'S BUREAU
speechtext:
1.	Is there any branch or division of any department of the federal government corresponding to the women's bureau of the United States Department of Labor?
2.	Has consideration been given to the establishment of a women's bureau of the Department of Labour here in Canada?
3.	Have any representations been received by the government asking for the establishing of a women's bureau? If so, from whom, and under what dates?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR
subsubtopic: WOMEN'S BUREAU
speechtext:
1.	In Canada there is no federally-operated agency which is comparable to the women's bureau of the United States department of labor.
There is, however, a division of the national employment service which corresponds to a degree with the women's bureau of the United States department of labor. This division is headed at head office by an adviser on women's employment. A brief statement of her duties is as follows:
(a)	To deal with the special interest/', and problems of women in relation tc their interests in the employment field.
(b)	To develop and maintain liaison with women's national organizations which are interested in the employment of women.
(c)	To represent women and to advise on the woman's viewpoint in regard to the establishment of policies and procedures in the national employment service.
(d)	To functionally supervise all operations of the service dealing with women.
(e)	Administrative and consultive duties dealing with the general administration of the service and with special projects such as female displaced persons, domestic service, et cetera.
There are similar positions at regional level, and the commission's policy is to have female officers deal with women in so far as possible. Where the volume warrants it, women's supervisors are female; and where the supervision is over a joint male and female function, the supervisory position is open to either males or females on equal terms.
2.	The needs of the service are constantly under review.
3.	Yes. From the Young Women's Christian Association, in 1945; from the National Council of Women, in 1945 and in 1946.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
I notice that this section reads:
No right, title or interest in or to public lands shall be acquired by any person by prescription.
Then the note on the other side of the page says:
Title by prescription has been abolished in many provinces under the provincial land titles acts.
It does not say that all the provinces have that condition. I am under the impression that in Newfoundland at least there is no such act. Is the minister in a position to say how many provinces have a provincial land titles act which applies? Because if it does not apply, the effect of this section will be to bring in a prescription act that will affect property rights in a province in which a provincial land titles act does not apply.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not familiar with the particular situation in Newfoundland. I will attempt to obtain the information. This regulation with respect to prescription states that, where people occupy land for a period

of sixty years, the land in effect became theirs. That is being abolished under this act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: Is that not interfering with the jurisdiction of the provinces with respect to property rights? People who now have prescriptive rights on property will have their rights interfered with.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that clause 7 quite clearly may take away certain rights. I also suggest one obvious mistake in the wording. I shall read the clause:
Such of the lands mentioned in the schedule to the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act as at the commencement of this act are vested in His Majesty in right of Canada, by whatever mode of conveyance they were acquired or taken, whether in fee, for life, for years or for otherwise,-
The word "for" is obviously wrong.
-and all appurtenances thereof, are and continue absolutely vested in His Majesty for the purposes of Canada.
I suggest that what this means is that a title which may now be conveyed for years, as indicated in the earlier part of the section, by reason of these unqualified words at the end, "are and continue absolutely vested in His Majesty," might very well be altered to extend the rights of the crown in a way that was never intended. I suggest there
2360	HOUSE OF
Public Lands Grants Act should be words added to the section to indicate that they are to be vested in His Majesty -some such words as these: for all of His Majesty's right, title and interest therein. Otherwise I suggest what you are doing is making what is now a partial title into an absolute title.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
This section as drafted carries the judgment of course of the Department of Justice, and is, I believe, almost word for word a reproduction of section 2 of the old act, the act respecting ordnance and admiralty lands, which reads:
All the lands mentioned in the schedule to this act, by whatever mode of conveyance the same have been acquired or taken, whether in fee, for life, for years or otherwise, and all the appurtenances thereof, are and shall be and continue absolutely vested in His Majesty for the purposes of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not
interested in what other section there may be in another act. What I am interested iri finding out is what this section means. What I want the minister to tell me is whether there is any substance in what I have said.
I think there is. I have consulted with one lawyer of some eminence on these words. I want an answer, not merely a statement that it is in another section. So far as I can see on the face of it, it is wrong. I want an answer which has some reasoning attached to it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: As I understood the hon. member's question, it was whether or not this was correct and did what it purported to do. My answer is that in my understanding and to the best of the judgment of the Department of Justice, it does.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: That again is a general assurance which carries very little value. I should like to see a definite opinion from the Department of Justice that indicates no such result as I suggest would ensue. If there is such an opinion, if this point has been considered, perhaps I can be answered, but I have not been answered yet. I may say, Mr. Chairman, there have been times, even in my short time in parliament, when governments were prepared to consider suggestions made from other quarters; but so far as I can see they are not even prepared to consider them now.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that remark was called for. We have treated the hon. member with deference, the deference which he deserves, because I think he is always anxious to improve, if he can, the legislative language that is used in the statutes we propose. I do not think he listened carefully to what the minister said. The minister said that in the Ordnance and


Admiralty Lands Act there was a provision which declared that all the lands mentioned in the schedule, at whatever date they had been conveyed to the crown, were vested absolutely in the crown. That is a statute that has been in existence over the years. This has to do only with those lands, and purports to say that they will continue to be vested in the crown. That is, those that were declared by the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act to be and to continue to be vested in the crown are being declared by this section, which replaces it, to continue to be vested in the crown. It is not something having a new effect; it is something which continues the effect of chapter 115 of the revised statutes, which itself was a revision of a prior act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister this question. After all, no one questions the Prime Minister's standing in the legal profession. Does the Prime Minister think there is nothing' in the suggestion which I have made, that as this matter stands it might very easily convey a title which, though covered by the previous act, may still be a title for years, and can by these words be turned into an absolute title? Will the Prime Minister say whether, if there is no possibility of that, there would be the slightest objection to putting in the proper words to indicate that the title, which is to remain in the crown, is merely such title as they have had? That is my whole point, and I think the Prime Minister appreciates it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: If this were new legislation we might be concerned about the possibility of its being construed as changing the title; but if the title was changed it was changed years ago by the previous statute. This is merely a repetition of what was in the previous statute. It is not new legislation. It was so drafted by the Department of Justice, which does, I think, endeavour to avoid in its drafting doing anything to which attention is not directed. May I send over to the hon. member the provision in the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act? This applies only to the lands mentioned in the schedule to the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act. It is the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act which was in force before the last revision of the statutes in 1927, and which, when it was originally adopted, might have been open to the objection the hon. member suggests; but that is something that was done I do not know how many years ago. This section merely restates what has been the effect of the other act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the Prime Minister says, as I understand he does, Mr. MAY 10. 1950
Chairman, that this point which I raise may have been perfectly relevant and proper and practical at the time the previous statute was enacted, then I want to ask this question. Is it not possible there may still be instances of land held for a term of years, which under this continuation as we now have it, and which I assume does replace the present act, may be changed? Is there any reason, if we made a mistake a considerable number of years ago, why we should perpetuate it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: I am not conceding that there was any mistake made. This applies only to the lands that were described in the schedule to the previous act, and the previous act had the same language that is to be found here. If that is language which operates, it operated a great many years ago when the original statute was passed, and if it was something which could modify a title, the modification took place several years ago. There are no others than these with respect to which it did take place several years ago which can be affected by this new provision of the present bill. If the hon. member will just look at chapter 115 of the revised statutes he will find that, comparing the drafts of both, this does not and cannot do anything new.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: Do I correctly understand that the Prime Minister is saying that regardless of the nature of the title, whether in fee, for life, for years or otherwise, which was vested.in the crown at the date of the coming into effect of the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act with respect to the lands in the schedule, the effect of that act was to vest in His Majesty in right of Canada an absolute title to these lands?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: No; my reading of it was that it merely vested in His Majesty the title that had been conveyed to His Majesty. Perhaps there might be grounds for another interpretation of the language that was used in the original Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act. But if there was, that is past history. If it was something which could change a title, the change was made a very long time ago, and no change is being made at this time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext:
With respect, it seems to me we are left in this dilemma, that if the effect of the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act with respect to these lands was to vest absolute title in His Majesty in right of Canada, then these succeeding words in the present section 7 are quite unnecessary. All that would be needed would be a declaratory statement that the lands in effect continue to be absolutely vested in His Majesty. The other horn of the dilemma is this, that if
Public Lands Grants Act absolute title was not vested in His Majesty in right of Canada by the Ordnance and Admiralty Lands Act, then it would be only fair and proper that this section should not go any further, and that it should be followed by some such words as, "for all the right, title and interest of His Majesty therein and thereto."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think there can be any legal objection to adding as many words as you like to say that this does not give any greater title than existed in His Majesty at the date of the sanction of this act. If it is felt that such words should go in, it would not have any effect, in my view, but having no effect the additional words could not do any harm. If it will ease anyone's mind to have it stated that they are and continue absolutely vested in His Majesty for the purposes of Canada in the same manner and to the same extent as at the date of the passage of this act, then I can see no objection to putting in those words. I do not think that it is wise to add unnecessary words, but if hon. members feel they are desirable, there can be no objection to putting them in-because that is the purpose, merely to have these lands continue to be vested to the same extent that they are vested at the present time. Perhaps the words would be, "in the same manner and to the same extent as at the time of the coming into force of this act."

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO CONVEYANCE, LEASES, DEFENCE LANDS, ETC.
speechtext: If the Prime Minister will agree to that, I should be very glad to see those words introduced. I do suggest that the word "for" in the fifth line, before the word "otherwise", should not have crept in. Would the minister care to make that alteration?

speechtext:
Subsection 1 states:
Public lands that are declared by the governor in council to be necessary for the defence of Canada shall not be sold, alienated or otherwise disposed of but may be leased or otherwise used as the governor in council thinks best for the advantage of Canada.
I should like to ask two questions of the minister which arise in connection with specific pieces of defence lands which I know have been considered for sale. I do not mind mentioning them; they are the Long Branch rifle range, which is just outside Toronto, and situated at the present time on an extremely valuable piece of building property in a built-up area. Representations have been made by the municipal authorities to the Department of National Defence for the release of these lands for building or industrial sites. I understand also that the small arms factory in that location, as well as the military camp used during the war, and which is now a housing project, are also situated on defence lands.

subtopic: REVISION AND REPEAL OF DOMINION LANDS ACT
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING SALE OR LEASE, ETC.
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to revise the Dominion Lands Act and bring it up to date under the name of the Territorial Lands Act. In the process of this revision all outdated and unnecessary provisions have been dropped. The Dominion Lands Act, originally enacted in 1872, was designed to assist in the proper and orderly development of the west and to provide appropriate regulations in connection with homesteading, the use of patents, and related matters. After the transfer of natural resources to the prairie provinces in 1930, however, the application of the Dominion Lands Act was restricted to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory.

The act as it stands does not suit conditions prevailing at the present time in the territories. It is considered desirable, therefore, to place in one measure all the powers of the Department of Resources and Development necessary for dealing with crown lands under its administration in the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory except, of course, lands under the Indian Act and lands in the national parks.
Since no homestead entry was ever permitted in the Northwest Territories, and since the practice of allowing homestead entry in Yukon Territory was discontinued some years ago, the sections of the act dealing with homesteading are now obsolete. Other portions of this legislation ,which have also become obsolete relate to school lands and Hudson's Bay land, provisions which applied only to the provinces. Provisions relating to the holding of public competitions for the right to cut timber in berths were discontinued many years ago; the practice at present is to issue a permit and to charge dues for the timber cut.
The proposed new act will apply to all lands in the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory under the control of the Department of Resources and Development, but will not in any way limit the operation of the Yukon Placer Mining Act, the Yukon Quartz Mining Act, the Dominion Water Power Act, or the National Parks Act. There is only part of one national park in the Northwest Territories, namely Wood Buffalo park.
In addition to repealing the Dominion Lands Act this bill also repeals the Irrigation Act and Reclamation Act. The Irrigation Act is now in force only in the district of Keewatin, where it has no practical application. The Reclamation Act applies only to vacant dominion land in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan; since the transfer to these provinces of all vacant dominion land, it has no practical application.

I should like to ask the minister why he decided upon -that policy? I should like to explain to him that if ore is discovered in that area and a mine is developed, the surface rights are almost completely subjected to the. mining operation. In regard to oil I think the law ought to be made as generous as possible to encourage people to prospect for oil. I have been informed that at Norman Wells in the Northwest Territories there are approximately 31 million barrels of oil in reserve. There are 62 wells which have been capped, and one well is now being used to supply a small refinery. This oil field is merely a continuation of the field at Leduc, and simply because it happens to be just on +he other side of the Yukon border or the

Northwest Territories border is no reason why any reservations should be placed upon it. It should be made available to those who search for oil.
At the moment a pipe line is in existence in the Yukon Territory. We have heard a lot of chaff about pipe lines in this house, but the only pipe line of any consequence in this country is the one running from Skagway to Whitehorse and 500 miles north to Fairbanks, Alaska. It is not an allCanadian route because it begins in Skagway, continues into Canada, and then goes on to Fairbanks, Alaska. The oil resources of the Northwest Territories are likely to exceed those of the province of Alberta, and the world should be invited to come in to search for and develop this valuable resource. Again this looms large in the defence of our country. We are all familiar with the fact that this very field which I mentioned was drawn upon during the war to supply the American refinery at Whitehorse, and the United States navy in the Pacific, at a time when the Japanese were in the Aleutians. One refinery has been dismantled and sent to the Leduc field, but the oil wells are there and can be called upon at any time in the defence of this continent. I say that prospectors for oil, oil companies, pipe line companies and so on should be encouraged to pay attention to the Northwest Territories.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to extend the provision of the Northwest Territories Power Commission Act to the Yukon Territory. The Northwest Territories power commission was established by statute in 1948 to construct and operate power plants in the Northwest Territories.
The commission has since October, 1948, operated on a self-sustaining basis a hydroelectric power development on the Snare river 94 miles northwest of Yellowknife, and now supplies power to gold mines at Yellowknife and to the Yellowknife Power Company Limited for distribution in the town of Yellowknife. Power is supplied at a cost calculated to meet operation and maintenance costs and interest charges on capital investment, and to amortize the capital cost over a period of twenty years.
At the present time the commission is constructing and will have in operation during the present year a plant to provide dieselgenerated electric power at Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories, which will supply electric power on a financially self-sustaining basis to the town of Fort Smith and to the various federal government establishments located there. A similar plant will be constructed at Hay River in the Northwest Territories, and it is expected that it too will be in operation before the end of the present year.
From the earliest days of settlement in the Yukon, mining has been a vitally important industrial activity of the territory. It remains so today. As this industry grows, the need for electric power will increase. On the other hand, the availability of power would encourage and stimulate the mining industry. Both the extraction and processing of ore would be made easier and more economical.
The Northwest Territories power commission is functioning efficiently and it is considered inadvisable to establish another authority to supervise and administer any proposed development and distribution of electric power in the neighbouring territory.
The whole purpose of this bill, therefore, is to extend the application of the Northwest 55946-151
Northwest Territories
Territories Power Commission Act to Yukon Territory, and thus enable the commission, whose operations in the Northwest Territories have been of considerable value toward the development of the mining industry in that part of Canada, to render a similar service in the Yukon.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllraiih (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO ARTICLES OF PALLADIUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1906 the Gold and Silver Stamping Act was passed] to provide for the accurate stamping of articles made of these metals. This became known as the Gold and Silver Marking Act in 1913, and in order to include platinum, which was becoming increasingly important in jewelry production, the act was amended in 1928 to include this metal, and became the Precious Metals Marking Act. Various amendments were made in

later years, and in 1946 those amendments were consolidated and the act generally revised.
Briefly, the purpose of the act is to provide that when articles composed of, or plated with, gold, silver or platinum are marked, such markings shall indicate the actual quality of the metal content. Licences are issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce to manufacturers to permit the use of the national mark on articles made of gold or silver and wholly of Canadian manufacture.
The Department of Trade and Commerce maintains a constant check on applied quality marks, and makes tests to ascertain the fineness of precious metals in articles. As a result, the illegal description of articles manufactured of gold, silver and platinum has practically disappeared. The group of metals classed as precious include gold, silver, platinum, palladium, ruthenium, rhodium, osmium and iridium. Until recently only gold, silver and platinum were used commercially to any extent. Palladium is a white metallic element of the platinum group. It is produced in Canada, and is a by-product of nickel refining. The by-products from such refining contain metals of the platinum family in a manner in which further refining is necessary.
In its pure state palladium is malleable and ductile, and is slightly harder than either gold or platinum. It can be hardened for jewelry manufacture by the addition of small amounts of other metal, usually ruthenium. This produces an all-platinum metal alloy that is resistible to wear, has the strength and toughness to retain gems permanently, is highly resistant to tarnish, and will retain a brilliant polish. Recently the jewelry industry has started the manufacture of articles composed of palladium. As it is the view of the industry that the use of this metal will likely increase as time goes on, it is desirable that it be brought within the provisions of the Precious Metals Marking Act, and that is the purpose of the present bill.

maintopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO ARTICLES OF PALLADIUM
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I want to make one or two brief general observations on the Precious Metals Marking Act. I did so when the act was under consideration in 1946, and the minister then piloting the bill through the house said he would give consideration to my suggestions.
The principle is very good, and there can be no objection whatever to having articles of jewelry, particularly, stamped with the fineness of the precious metal used in making the object. However, I believe a strong case could be made for the adoption of a Canadian hall-mark. This act, in common 55946-1511
Precious Metals Marking Act with the 1946 act, merely states that the fineness of the metal shall be stamped on a piece of jewelry, for instance. It does not provide that the jewelry shall be stamped with the date, the country of origin, or anything else. The English hall-mark, and some of the continental hall-marks, though not to the same extent, are extremely valuable and useful methods of marking articles made of precious metals, particularly gold and silver. As the age of the object increases, so does its value. These hall-marks enable those concerned to ascertain where the article was made, when it was made, and other pertinent facts concerning it, whereas under our system we merely designate the type of metal and the fineness.
I mention this point for the reason that in Canada today the goldsmithing and silver-smithing industry is increasing rapidly, and a great deal of the very finest jewelry as well as flatware, silver, cutlery, and other things are now made in this country. In order to encourage this industry, and in order to show the rest of the world that we in Canada do produce high quality articles of great artistry, I believe a Canadian hallmark should be devised which would not only show the fineness of the metal but also the year of manufacture and the fact that it was made in Canada. I feel that by including these markings on precious metals we would be aiding our craftsmen and our precious metals industry. We would also be advertising throughout the world the fact that we in Canada had a goldsmiths' and silversmiths' industry of which we were proud.
I mention that because the International Nickel Company, which advertises all over the world, is now making a special advertising drive in some of the quality papers of the United States concerning the use of this metal palladium. It is said to be one of the most useful metals for the setting of jewels. I think it would be of assistance if metals such as palladium were marked as being of Canadian origin by having a "C", or some other insignia, stamped upon it. I suggest that to the parliamentary assistant as a means of encouraging our own industry, and advertising our own craftsmen.
